title: Museum strings together 30 old Mac minis for replica of most successful supercomputer, builds something more powerful than the original
summary: Happy birthday, Apple.
body: What's better than giving the hardware you already own a fresh lease on life ? Dedicating your older tech to resurrecting even older supercomputers. At least, that's if you ask the Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain . The hardware history museum recently used 30 Mac Minis dating between 2012 and 2014 to resurrect the Cray-1 supercomputer (via Ars Technica ). Debuting in the bygone year of 1976, the Cray-1 is noted for its striking C-shaped cabinet. However, what's arguably most impactful about the new display is that its composite parts make it technically more powerful than the original machine. The museum's exhibit features five quad-core i7s, and 25 dual-core i5s, resulting in a total of 70 cores to play with. The 30 Mac Minis run on Mojave, leveraging MacOS' Message Passing Interface to pass off computing tasks between them. When all of these cores were online during testing, the exhibit achieved 1.5 teraflops. The original Cray-1 had a 64-bit, 80 MHz processor and 8.39 MB of memory (PDF warning), with a theoretical peak performance of about 160 megaflops. body: One of the many ways AI will (supposedly) revolutionise the games industry is facilitating highly reactive NPCs via LLM-powered chatbots. Yet so far, only a handful of games like Where Winds Meet have attempted to implement the tech, and the results have been less than spectacular. But there might also be another reason why relatively few games feature LLM-powered NPCs, which is that powering such chatbots can be costly, as recently demonstrated by the developers of an upcoming driving instructor simulator As reported by FRVR (via Kotaku ) Teach My Little Sister How To Drive is a comic simulation game in which you coach your virtual sibling on driving technique from the comfort of the passenger seat. The twist is that behind your sister's dinner-plate eyes is an LLM chatbot (currently powered by an OpenAI model, though the developers intend to use Gemini for the final release) In the role of instructor, players can both converse with the chatbot and issue vocal instructions such as "turn left here", to which the bot will respond accordingly. title: Deadlock's City Never Sleeps update makes Valve's MOBA my favorite videogame setting in years
summary: I wanna be a part of it, New York, New York.
body: Play This Right Now Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. You can subscribe to the newsletter at the link if you want to get our thoughts about a new videogame happening direct to your inbox every Thursday. Deadlock isn't technically out yet—but it's pretty easy to get into, with invites to its beta being generously granted by Valve and obtainable in plenty of Discord communities if you don't have other mates who're into MOBA s. And boy howdy, have I not regretted a single one of my 350 hours over the past couple years "testing" this game. I've plenty of glowing words for Deadlock, but its latest update, City Never Sleeps, is like seeing one of the last few hammer-blows of a masterpiece. The entire map's been completely overhauled , with new neutral monsters and a richly-textured remake of its areas, though "remake" doesn't seem like the right word. title: It looks like Wing Commander 3 is getting a remaster, after EA producer discovers the original FMV source tapes in the company's archives
summary: Plans for a 30th Anniversary Edition of the classic space sim were revealed at Portland Gaming Expo.
body: Typical, isn't it? You wait ages for new information on a Chris Roberts-directed space combat sim, and then two lots come along at once. Less than 24 hours after Cloud Imperium Games surprise-released a glossy trailer for Star Citizen 's single-player spinoff Squadron 42, it now appears that Roberts' 1994 classic Wing Commander 3 is getting a remaster courtesy of EA. The project is headed up by EA producer Jim Vessella, who revealed the remaster during a presentation at the Portland Retro Gaming Expo . The remaster will include cutscenes based on Wing Commander 3's original FMV recordings, after Vessella discovered 600 source tapes while digitising EA's video archive. In a post on Bluesky, Steve Lin, a board member of the Video Game History Foundation , shared an image of Vessella's talk , which shows a projector slide detailing the remaster's features. The remaster is called Wing Commander 3: Heart of the Tiger—30 th anniversary edition. A slightly unfortunate name, given Wing Commander 3's was released 32 years ago. title: Deadlock surpasses Team Fortress 2's all-time concurrent player count peak as it adds a chess wizard
summary: Siri, call my pawns.
body: Valve's latest MOBA might still technically be conducting an invite-only test, but it's nevertheless one of the most popular games of its ilk. Yesterday, right as the game added the latest in its current batch of six new democratically released heroes , its concurrent player-count hit a new screaming high: 262,145 simultaneous players, according to SteamDB . While that's pretty impressive on its face, it'll be especially noteworthy to long-time fans of Valve's games that this surge of activity brought Deadlock past Team Fortress 2's all-time concurrent player count peak of 253,997. Though this doesn't include the player numbers TF2 saw on the Xbox 360 and PS3 as part of The Orange Box, which I'm sure were positively through the roof, it's still conceivably its genuine peak given that it was just three years ago. As for how TF2's history of botting issues and idle servers might have affected that number, I can't say. title: The studio behind Star Wars Zero Company is bringing back some of its furloughed staff
summary: "[The furlough] was an incredibly difficult decision, but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring back as many people as possible."
body: Just as Star Wars Zero Company was set to launch earlier this year, developer Bit Reactor furloughed over 80% of its staff over sales uncertainty . In other words, much of its staff were receiving no pay, despite technically being employees, right when players were getting their hands on the game. Earlier this week on Bluesky , the studio announced it had begun undoing this "difficult decision" (via gamesindustry.biz ). Bit Reactor CEO Greg Foertsch said in the statement that the decision was made in response to "unexpected business developments outside of our control," but that it was "necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible." According to Game File , an unnamed source "familiar with the situation" has said that the developer's payroll is back up to more than half what it was before the furloughs. When this first happened, Game File reported that 80 percent of Bit Reactor employees were affected, hamstringing any sort of support following the game's release, and that the decision fell with Bit Reactor, not publisher EA. title: The advent of first-person shooters introduced a wild frontier of unregulated video game level packs, and it ended in a lawsuit that changed copyright forever
summary: Revisiting the forgotten fourth state of PC gaming.
body: Weird Weekend Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh and Rick have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager . For most of PC gaming history, there were three states of PC game—your regular old video game, expansions/DLC, and mods. But for a brief period in the 1990s, there was a fourth state, the level pack—collections of levels for the early first-person shooters like Duke Nukem 3D and Quake . These level packs were sold on shelves as boxed products just like their video game counterparts. But they occupied a far more amorphous position between the other three states of PC gaming. In form and structure, they were similar to expansions, and are sometimes bundled into the same category. The Master Levels for Doom 2, for example, are regarded as an official expansion to that game. body: Silent Hill's resurrection is one of the happier stories to emerge from the games industry in recent years. After spending roughly a decade locked in a Konami cupboard, Silent Hill has received three new entries published by Konami in as many years, all of which arrived to positive reviews and, seemingly, healthy sales. But if Silent Hill 2 Remake, Silent Hill f , and Silent Hill: Townfall still haven't satisfied your craving for allegorical horror in foggy towns, fret not, because Konami has plenty more plans for the series' ongoing revival. In an interview featured in Famitsu (via IGN ), Silent Hill producer Motoi Okamoto explained that Konami is "relieved" by both the critical and commercial reception to the aforementioned three games. "All three titles we initially announced were able to be released successfully," Okamoto said, adding that, "they've also received high praise, and we are satisfied with it." Okamoto went on to say that the games released so far only represent the "first wave" of Konami's planned games for the series, and that there's not one but two additional waves on the drawing board. title: 'If you're skilful enough, you can chop the head off a monster, kick it midair, and then kill another monster with it': Consider me sold on this indie first-person ARPG
summary: Heathen puts a new perspective on Diablo, and it looks brilliant.
body: Certain ideas that crop up every so often in games will always grab my attention. One of them is letting players defeat enemies with bits of other enemies. As such, my interest in Heathen—an upcoming indie dungeon crawler—went from 'mildly curious' to 'smashing the wishlist button' when its most recent trailer revealed you can beat your foes by volleying other enemy heads at them. Developed by solo developer Christoper Yabsley, Heathen takes the frantic monster bashing and loot hoarding of Diablo and reworks it for a first-person perspective. Set in the fantasy town of Saltgrave, it sees your character seeking fortune and glory in the vast subterranean labyrinth beneath the town, encountering an "ancient horror" in the process in what the Steam page describes as a "descent into madness." The chief addition that the trailer explores is a new enemy dismemberment system added by Yabsley, which he says has "done a lot for making swords and axes feel really good".
